lead: This unit builds the language of the IC engine: what kinds there are, what the parts are called and made of, how four-stroke and two-stroke, SI and CI engines work, when the valves and ports open, in what order the cylinders fire, and how the ideal, fuel-air and actual cycles predict efficiency. After it you can classify any engine, draw its timing diagrams and work an Otto, Diesel or dual cycle to the mean effective pressure.
about: The unit moves from the machine to its thermodynamics. It starts with the history and classification of engines and the names and materials of their parts, then follows the piston through the four-stroke and two-stroke cycles and through the SI and CI ways of starting combustion. Valve and port timing diagrams show when the gas actually moves, and firing order and valve gear show how a multi-cylinder engine is organised. The last two chapters replace the engine by ideal cycles (Otto, Diesel and dual), then add the real working fluid (the fuel-air cycle) and the real losses read from the indicator diagram. Each chapter uses the words and numbers of the ones before it: the cylinder of the terminology chapter reappears in the cycle calculations.

chapters.idea: An IC engine burns fuel inside its cylinder to make work, and its many types are sorted by independent choices such as ignition, stroke and cooling.
chapters.depth: Cover engine types and operation: reciprocating and rotary; SI and CI; four-stroke and two-stroke; air-cooled and water-cooled; naturally aspirated and supercharged; common fuels. Give a short history with Lenoir, Otto, Diesel and Clerk, one line each. Multi-stroke engines: only a few universities teach this, so keep it to a short advanced note. Do not derive cycles here.

figure.aria: A classification tree sorts IC engines by ignition, stroke, cooling and aspiration.

chapters.example: Question: A two-wheeler engine is petrol-fuelled, spark-ignition, two-stroke, air-cooled and naturally aspirated, with a stated displacement of 150 cm³. Classify it under five headings and name one vehicle use. Answer: fuel = petrol; ignition = SI; stroke = two-stroke; cooling = air; aspiration = natural. Use: a scooter.
chapters.trap: Do not mix independent axes: a two-stroke engine is not the same as a two-cylinder engine, and a diesel engine is not always the same as a CI engine in every context.
chapters.leave: Detailed cycles go to Chapter 1.7; components go to Chapter 1.2; timing goes to Chapter 1.5.

chapters.idea: Standard geometry terms and each component's function and material give the fixed language for all later engine calculations.
chapters.depth: Define bore, stroke, TDC, BDC, swept volume, clearance volume, compression ratio and mean effective pressure. Give component functions and typical materials: cylinder block (cast iron), piston (aluminium alloy), rings (cast iron or steel), gudgeon pin, connecting rod (forged steel), crankshaft (alloy steel), flywheel, valves, camshaft, spark plug or injector, cylinder head and crankcase. Some syllabi call this constructional details.

figure.aria: A component tree groups the main engine parts by their job in holding, moving or controlling gas flow.

chapters.example: Question: A four-cylinder engine has bore 80 mm, stroke 90 mm and clearance volume 62.8 cm³ per cylinder. Find one-cylinder swept volume, total displacement and compression ratio. Answer: d = 8.0 cm, L = 9.0 cm. Swept volume = (π/4) × 8.0² × 9.0 = 452.4 cm³. Total displacement = 4 × 452.4 = 1809.6 cm³, about 1.81 L. Compression ratio = (452.4 + 62.8) / 62.8 = 8.20.
chapters.trap: Compression ratio is not swept volume divided by clearance volume; it is (swept + clearance) divided by clearance. Keep mm and cm consistent in the area formula.
chapters.leave: Combustion details go to Unit 3; cooling and lubrication go to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A four-stroke engine uses four piston strokes and two revolutions per cycle, while a two-stroke engine uses ports and one revolution per cycle with scavenging.
chapters.depth: Four-stroke: intake, compression, power and exhaust, with two crankshaft revolutions per cycle. Two-stroke: one revolution, piston-controlled ports, transfer and scavenging. Compare power strokes per revolution, smoothness, fuel consumption, emissions and cooling needs. Name uniflow and loop scavenging only; details go to Unit 4.

figure.aria: A timeline compares the four-stroke cycle, with one power stroke in 720 crank degrees, and the two-stroke cycle, with one power stroke in 360 crank degrees.

chapters.example: Question: A four-stroke engine runs at 3000 rpm. Find the number of power strokes per second per cylinder and the time for one complete cycle. Repeat for a two-stroke engine at the same speed. Answer: 3000 rpm = 50 rev/s. Four-stroke: one power stroke per 2 revolutions, so 25 power strokes/s; cycle time = 2 / 50 = 0.040 s. Two-stroke: one power stroke per revolution, so 50 power strokes/s; cycle time = 1 / 50 = 0.020 s.
chapters.trap: A two-stroke engine does not complete a cycle in two strokes of one revolution in the same sense as a four-stroke; it has one power stroke per revolution and uses ports, not only valves.
chapters.leave: Scavenging details go to Unit 4; combustion stages go to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: An SI engine ignites a premixed fuel-air charge with a spark, while a CI engine injects fuel into hot compressed air and relies on autoignition.
chapters.depth: SI: premixed charge, throttle control, spark plug, flame propagation, lower compression ratio. CI: air-only intake, high compression ratio, injector, fuel-air mixing, autoignition. Compare efficiency, torque, emissions and typical compression ratios. Mention spark timing and injection timing as events, not full systems; those belong to Unit 2.

figure.aria: Two parallel block paths show SI ignition of a premixed charge by spark and CI injection into hot air for autoignition.

chapters.example: Question: An SI engine has compression ratio 9 and a CI engine has compression ratio 18. Both have clearance volume 50 cm³. Find the swept volume of each. Answer: swept volume = (compression ratio − 1) × clearance volume. SI: (9 − 1) × 50 = 400 cm³. CI: (18 − 1) × 50 = 850 cm³.
chapters.trap: A CI engine compresses air only, not a fuel-air mixture. Do not say the spark plug and injector are interchangeable; they mark different ignition paths.
chapters.leave: Fuel supply and ignition systems go to Unit 2; knock and combustion stages go to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Valve and port timing diagrams show when gas passages open and close relative to TDC and BDC, including lead, lag and overlap.
chapters.depth: Valve timing for SI and CI engines: inlet opens before TDC and closes after BDC; exhaust opens before BDC and closes after TDC; show valve overlap. Port timing for two-stroke engines: exhaust, transfer and inlet ports open and close in crank degrees. Compare SI and CI valve timing as a tutorial. Some syllabi call these valve and port timing diagrams.

figure.aria: A 720-degree timeline shows inlet and exhaust open periods, valve overlap near TDC, and spark and injection near the end of compression.

chapters.example: Question: A four-stroke SI engine has inlet valve opening 10° before TDC and closing 40° after BDC; exhaust valve opening 45° before BDC and closing 10° after TDC. Find the inlet open period, exhaust open period and valve overlap in crank degrees. Answer: inlet = 10 + 180 + 40 = 230°; exhaust = 45 + 180 + 10 = 235°; overlap = 10 + 10 = 20°.
chapters.trap: Timing angles are measured in crank degrees, not cam degrees unless stated. Do not add overlap twice; it is the common open period around TDC.
chapters.leave: Valve actuation and firing order go to Chapter 1.6; scavenging details go to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Firing order, valve layout and valve actuation decide the sequence and smoothness of power pulses and how the valves are moved.
chapters.depth: Firing order: definition, significance, common four-cylinder orders 1-3-4-2 and 1-2-4-3; firing interval = 720/n for a four-stroke. Valve layouts: L-head, T-head, I-head and F-head; OHV, OHC and DOHC. Valve actuation: camshaft, pushrod, rocker, belt or chain drive, hydraulic lifter. Variable valve timing only as a recent development; keep cam profile design out.

figure.aria: Four firing events are spaced 180 crank degrees apart in the order 1-3-4-2.

chapters.example: Question: A four-cylinder four-stroke engine fires in the order 1-3-4-2 at 2400 rpm. Find the firing interval in crank degrees and the time between successive firings. Answer: interval = 720 / 4 = 180°. 2400 rpm = 40 rev/s. 180° is half a revolution, so time = 0.5 / 40 = 0.0125 s = 12.5 ms.
chapters.trap: For a four-stroke engine use 720/n for firing interval, not 360/n. A different firing order keeps the same interval but changes balance and manifold behaviour.
chapters.leave: Valve timing diagrams are in Chapter 1.5; detailed cam design is outside this unit.

chapters.idea: Ideal air-standard cycles replace combustion by heat addition and use air as the working fluid so Otto, Diesel and dual cycles can be compared fairly.
chapters.depth: Air-standard assumptions: fixed air mass, ideal gas, constant specific heats, closed cycle, no intake or exhaust. Otto: constant-volume heat addition, efficiency = 1 − 1/r^(γ−1). Diesel: constant-pressure heat addition with cut-off ratio ρ. Dual cycle: both heat additions. Compare at the same compression ratio and same heat input; define mean effective pressure. Some syllabi call Otto the constant-volume cycle and Diesel the constant-pressure cycle.

figure.aria: A plot compares Otto and Diesel efficiency against compression ratio, with Diesel using a cut-off ratio of 2.

chapters.example: Question: An Otto cycle has compression ratio 8 and γ = 1.4. A Diesel cycle has the same compression ratio and cut-off ratio 2. Find both efficiencies. Answer: Otto η = 1 − 1/8^0.4 = 0.565 = 56.5%. Diesel η = 1 − (1/8^0.4) × ((2^1.4 − 1)/(1.4 × (2 − 1))) = 0.490 = 49.0%.
chapters.trap: The Diesel efficiency formula needs the cut-off ratio; do not use the Otto formula for a Diesel cycle. At the same compression ratio, Otto is more efficient than Diesel.
chapters.leave: Fuel-air and actual cycles go to Chapter 1.8; engine testing and performance go to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Fuel-air cycles keep the ideal cycle but use a real mixture and variable specific heats; actual cycle analysis adds gas exchange, heat loss and friction.
chapters.depth: Fuel-air cycle: real fuel-air mixture, variable specific heats, dissociation and finite combustion; still ideal and without friction. Actual cycle: valve timing, pumping loop, heat loss, blowdown, exhaust, friction and incomplete combustion; read an indicator diagram. Compare air-standard, fuel-air and actual efficiencies. Only a few universities teach the full loss breakdown; keep it short if your syllabus stops at fuel-air. Emissions are covered in Unit 6.

figure.aria: Nested sets place the air-standard cycle inside the fuel-air cycle inside the actual cycle, adding real-mixture and loss effects.

chapters.example: Question: An air-standard Otto cycle has efficiency 56.5%. A fuel-air cycle at the same compression ratio has efficiency 48.0%. The actual indicated efficiency is 38.0%. Find the fall from air-standard to fuel-air, from fuel-air to actual, and the overall fall. Answer: 56.5 − 48.0 = 8.5 percentage points; 48.0 − 38.0 = 10.0 percentage points; overall 56.5 − 38.0 = 18.5 percentage points.
chapters.trap: A fuel-air cycle is still an ideal cycle and has no friction. Friction and pumping losses belong to the actual cycle, so do not subtract them in the fuel-air step.
chapters.leave: Emission formation and control go to Unit 6; combustion stages go to Unit 3; testing and heat balance go to Unit 5.
